shape.name: Shape F - Productive Skills (Traditional)
shape.description: Traditional productive skills lesson with preparation stages followed by speaking or writing output.
shape.pedagogical_justification: Here the focus is on helping learners practice their speaking or writing skills. The lesson can usually be divided into preparation for speaking/writing and speaking/writing task stages.
shape.main_aim_format: By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to [speak/write] about [topic].

example_lesson_plan.header:
Objective:
By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to write a short response to a compare-and-contrast question, stating a clear position with a reason and a piece of evidence.
Teacher:
Ed Rush
Date:
05-08-26
Duration:
46 minutes
CEFR Level:
B1
Lesson Shape:
F (Productive Skills - Writing)
Materials:
Slideshow, essay question cards
Assessment:
Written response (opinion, reason, evidence)
Skills:
Writing, Speaking

stages.stage_aim: To activate students' prior knowledge of opinions and reasons, and to introduce the Opinion-Reason-Evidence frame
procedure: Show the splash slide. Ask: "What do you see? What might this lesson be about?" Let students guess.
Advance to the title slide: "Read the question. Take a position." Confirm the theme: today we start writing an opinion essay.
Show the "Why is this lesson important?" slide and read the bullets aloud.
Students work in pairs. Ask: "Cats or dogs — which makes a better pet?" Each student gives one reason. 2 minutes.
Elicit two or three opinions. Point to the Opinion-Reason-Evidence line at the bottom of the slide.

stages.stage_aim: To teach students to identify the four parts of a compare-and-contrast question
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "How do we read the question?"
Teach the strategy table: read the question twice; every question has four parts.
Show the anatomy slide: Context, Opinion A, Opinion B, Your choice. Check understanding of each part.
Project the teacher's conscription question on the matching slide. Students match each sentence to its part before you click.
Reveal the correct matches with auto-animate. Say each part aloud and confirm the colours.

stages.stage_aim: To show students that a good essay needs one clear opinion, and to model choosing a side
procedure: Teach the strategy table: choose one side; essays need one clear opinion; ask which side you agree with more.
Show the teacher's example on the demo slide. Ask: "Which side would the teacher choose?"
Click to reveal the green check mark. Emphasise that no side is wrong, but students must choose one.

stages.stage_aim: For students to apply the parsing strategy to their own randomly assigned question
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "Your turn."
Distribute one essay question card to each student at random. Students cannot choose their topic.
Project the task slide. Students read their question twice, underline the topic, circle both opinions, and choose their side.
Monitor and help students who cannot find both opinions.

stages.stage_aim: To introduce the hierarchy of evidence: statistics, quotations, news examples, personal anecdotes
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "How strong is your evidence?"
Teach the strategy table: support your reasons with evidence; strong evidence convinces the reader.
Reveal the evidence pyramid one level at a time, top-down: statistics, quotations, news examples, personal anecdotes.
Use the conscription examples on each level. Stress that statistics are strongest and anecdotes weakest.
Explain that students do not need statistics or quotations today, but they must know these levels exist.

stages.stage_aim: For students to write a three-sentence response: opinion, reason, and evidence
procedure: Show the scaffold slide with the sentence frames: I believe that..., One reason is..., For example, ...
Project the red task slide: "Write your response."
Students write three sentences: their opinion, one reason, and one piece of evidence about their own question card. 6 minutes.
Collect the responses at the end of the stage.

stages.stage_aim: For students to share their position orally using the Opinion-Reason-Evidence frame
procedure: Show the discussion-structure slide with the Opinion-Reason-Evidence table and the conscription example.
Students share their responses with a partner, using the frames: opinion, reason, evidence.
Elicit two or three strong examples for the whole class.
Show the wrap-up slide: "Your essay starts here." Preview lesson 2: building the full essay.

shape.note: For middle schoolers interested in SCR approach to productive skills, see Shape J instead.

metadata.topic: Compare and contrast essays: read the question, take a position
materials: Slideshow — Lesson 1: Read the Question, Take a Position
Essay question cards — 10 compare-and-contrast topics, randomly distributed
Teacher example: the conscription question (used for the parsing and position demos)
metadata.main_aim: By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to write a short response to a compare-and-contrast question, stating a clear position with a reason and a piece of evidence.
metadata.subsidiary_aim: Learners will also be better able to identify the four parts of an essay question and use the Opinion–Reason–Evidence frame when discussing their position.
answer_key: Context: Every year, Thai men must join the army for a short time.
Opinion A: Some people say the army builds discipline and national pride.
Opinion B: But others believe it wastes two years of young men's lives.
Your choice: Personally, I think military service is an essential commitment.
The teacher chooses Opinion A: military training builds discipline and national pride. Any side is valid — the point is to choose one side and defend it.
Statistics: A survey found that 7 in 10 young men feel fitter after army training.
Quotations: An officer said, "Army life taught me to be strong."
News examples: The news showed young men in uniform helping people after the floods.
Personal anecdotes: My uncle says the army made him fitter.
